This run covered 21 evals across 3 iterations each (111 total runs, 0 failed). Five evals ("cost-token-context-overflow", "neg-guardrail-false-positive", "neg-vpc-endpoint-timeout", "neg-kb-embedding-dimension", "neg-live-outage-503") were negative-trigger tests marked should_trigger:false and were skipped entirely for expected-output, assertions, metrics, comparison, and consistency — they contribute no comparative data, only confirming both variants correctly did not over-trigger (trigger_fired was 100% in those that reported it).

Across the 16 evals with real data, trigger_fired was consistently 3/3 (100%) for both variants except "direct-model-id-vs-profile" (2/3, 67%), which is a shared ceiling and not a point of difference between variants.

**Expected output and assertions.** On most evals, with_skill met the expected output notably more often than without_skill: e.g. "cost-throttle-default-quota" (3/3 vs 0/3), "quota-lookup-by-code" (3/3 vs 0/3), "tokens-per-day-quota" (3/3 vs 0/3), "invocation-log-retention" (3/3 vs 1/3), "billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained" (3/3 vs 0/3), "mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint" (3/3 vs 0/3), "quota-headroom" (2/3 vs 0/3), "cost-idle-provisioned-throughput" (3/3 vs 2/3), "cost-global-vs-geographic-profile" (3/3 vs 2/3), "per-model-cost-breakdown" (3/3 vs 1/3). This pattern holds at the assertion level too, with many "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" results and few in the reverse direction. Exceptions run the other way: "cost-throttle-tpm-vs-rpm" had without_skill meeting expected output 3/3 vs with_skill's 1/3 (though assertion pass rate favored with_skill, 90% vs 76%, showing expected-output and assertion-level measures can diverge). Two evals had both variants fail expected output entirely ("cost-unexpected-charge-spike" 0/3 vs 0/3, "cost-batch-vs-realtime" 0/3 vs 0/3), indicating the behavior/assertion itself may need work rather than reflecting a variant difference. "burndown-sum-not-maximum" had both variants pass expected output 3/3, with assertion pass rates close (75% vs 67%). Some individual assertions always passed for both (e.g. "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" in several evals) or always failed for both (e.g. the burstiness-distinguishing assertion in "cost-throttle-default-quota," the metrics-reading assertion in "cost-unexpected-charge-spike," the check-id assertion in "burndown-sum-not-maximum"), meaning those assertions don't differentiate the variants. Many "flaky" per-assertion patterns (passing some iterations, not others, for either variant) point to run-to-run variability rather than a stable skill gap. Confidence on expected-output judgments was generally high, though several were medium, and one ("quota-headroom", one assertion) was low — a reminder these are judgment calls, not hard facts.

**Runtime and cost.** No consistent directional pattern: with_skill was much slower/costlier in some evals (e.g. "cost-throttle-default-quota": 1m24s/$0.70 vs 10m29s/$5.23 — here without_skill was slower; "cost-global-vs-geographic-profile": 1m42s/$0.85 vs 50s/$0.42 — here with_skill was slower), while without_skill was dramatically slower/costlier in others ("quota-lookup-by-code": 15s/$0.13 vs 4m10s/$2.08; "quota-headroom": 44s/$0.37 vs 13m52s/$6.91; "tokens-per-day-quota": 18s/$0.15 vs 10m52s/$5.42; "cost-throttle-default-quota" also showed without_skill far slower). Runtime-threshold exceedances in the comparison data also appear for both variants depending on the eval. These swings are large in several cases and should be read alongside quality, not as a standalone penalty.

**Output quality comparisons (paired judgments).** Where pairs could be evaluated (many evals had 2-3 of 3 pairs skipped, so sample sizes are often very small, 0-3 pairs), the direction mostly favored with_skill (e.g. "cost-idle-provisioned-throughput" 7 vs 0; "cost-global-vs-geographic-profile" 5 vs 1; "burndown-sum-not-maximum" 5 vs 2; "per-model-cost-breakdown" 3 vs 0; "prompt-cache-payoff" 3 vs 0), with one clear exception where without_skill was favored 3-0 ("invocation-log-retention") and one near-even case ("cost-throttle-tpm-vs-rpm" 2 vs 1). Confidence on these quality judgments was mostly medium, sometimes high. Many evals had all 3 quality pairs skipped, meaning no quality comparison was possible there at all.

**Output consistency (run-to-run stability).** with_skill was rated "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" in most evals, occasionally "inconsistent" (e.g. "cost-unexpected-charge-spike," "cost-batch-vs-realtime," "prompt-cache-payoff"). without_skill showed a similar mix, also dipping to "inconsistent" in several evals (e.g. "cost-throttle-default-quota," "cost-unexpected-charge-spike," "mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint," "prompt-cache-payoff"). In "prompt-cache-payoff" both variants were rated fully "inconsistent" (score 1.0), indicating that eval's outputs vary a lot run-to-run for both. One eval ("direct-model-id-vs-profile") has no consistency score at all for with_skill (null), limiting comparison there.

**Overall pattern.** On the majority of evals with usable data, with_skill met expected outputs and passed assertions more often than without_skill, and quality judgments (where available) leaned toward with_skill as well, though sample sizes for quality were small and confidence often medium. Runtime and cost showed no single consistent direction — each variant was substantially slower/costlier than the other in different evals, sometimes by many minutes and several dollars. A few evals (two negative-ish "both fail expected output" cases, several "always fails" assertions, and one eval with both variants rated fully inconsistent) suggest some test behaviors or assertions are hard for either variant or the measurement itself is unstable, rather than reflecting one variant's weakness. Five evals contributed no comparative signal because they were skipped as not-applicable (should_trigger:false).

Overall, the evidence across expected-output matching, most individual assertions, runtime, cost, and output consistency points toward with_skill differing from without_skill in this task, but one assertion reversed that pattern (without_skill performed better) and one assertion failed for both, and the quality-comparison dimension produced no usable data at all. Overall picture: The two variants trade off across dimensions rather than one clearly outperforming the other. without_skill met the explicit expected-output criterion far more consistently and ran much faster and cheaper, while with_skill passed more individual assertions overall — though that gap is driven almost entirely by one specific metric-naming assertion, and a separate assertion (finding-sourcing) fails for both variants at the same rate. prompt-cache-payoff.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested a task involving reading cache token metrics by model and flagging cost findings (e.g., LLM-COST-002). The behavior under test fired reliably for both variants (3/3).

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in 2/3 runs (67%), without_skill in 1/3 (33%). Both measurements carry high confidence, so this gap is a reasonably solid signal, though it's based on only 3 runs each, which is a small sample.

Per-assertion detail (18 assertions total, 6 unique assertions x 3 runs): with_skill passed 14/18 (78%) vs without_skill's 7/18 (39%). Every one of the 6 assertions is flagged as "flaky" (inconsistent across the 3 repeats) for both variants, and on each individual assertion with_skill matched or outperformed without_skill - most notably on "identifies GPT-5.6 Terra as writing to cache without reading it back and raises LLM-COST-002," where with_skill passed 2/3 and without_skill passed 0/3. Two assertions (the "every finding carries a check-id" one and "no raw account ID exposed") were passed by with_skill in all 3 runs, with without_skill passing most but not all. No assertion favored without_skill over with_skill, and none passed uniformly for both (all show some failures), suggesting the underlying behavior is not yet fully reliable for either variant.

Quality comparison: only 1 of 3 pairs could actually be evaluated head-to-head (2 were skipped, likely due to inapplicability). In that single evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with high confidence. This is directionally informative but rests on just one comparable instance, so it should be read as a limited data point rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was substantially faster (avg 46s vs 2m8s) and cheaper (avg $0.38 vs $1.07), and used less context window (4.8% vs 12.2%, neither compacted). Only one runtime pair could be evaluated against the 30s threshold, and that one run exceeded it. This is a clear tradeoff: without_skill is markedly faster and cheaper, while with_skill showed higher expected-output match, higher assertion pass rate, and was favored in the one quality comparison available.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "inconsistent" across all three measured dimensions (score 1.0 inconsistency for both), with high confidence. Neither variant produced stable, repeatable outputs across runs — this is a shared weakness rather than a point of difference.

Overall, the picture is a tradeoff between speed/cost (favoring without_skill) and expected-output/assertion-pass-rate/quality (favoring with_skill), with both variants showing meaningful run-to-run inconsistency and most quality/runtime comparisons limited to very small sample sizes (often just one pair), which should temper confidence in how far these differences generalize.

direct-model-id-vs-profile.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested whether the agent correctly identifies direct (non-inference-profile) model invocation and raises an LLM-INV-002 finding with proper evidence.

Trigger: the behavior-under-test condition fired in 2 of 3 runs (67%), meaning for 1 of 3 runs there wasn't a valid test of this scenario at all — a notable limitation on how much can be concluded from only 3 attempts.

Expected output: neither variant met the expected output often. with_skill passed 1/3 (33%), without_skill passed 0/3 (0%). Both measurements are backed by high confidence, so the low pass rates reflect genuine judgments rather than noisy/low-confidence scoring. Overall this points to the underlying behavior (correctly flagging direct model invocation) being hard for both variants, with with_skill succeeding in a single run that without_skill did not match.

Assertions (18 checks across 6 unique assertion types, 3 runs each): with_skill passed 12/18 (67%) vs without_skill 8/18 (44%). Breaking down by assertion:
- Two assertions passed 3/3 for both variants ("does not raise LLM-INV-002 for a model with no profile" and "no raw account ID exposed") — these are not differentiating; both variants handle them reliably.
- One assertion ("every finding carries a proper check-id/severity and cited evidence") passed 3/3 for with_skill and 2/3 for without_skill — a small, single-run gap.
- Three assertions showed a consistent pattern where with_skill passed 1/3 and without_skill passed 0/3: correctly identifying the direct-call model and raising LLM-INV-002, basing the answer on account metrics/profiles rather than general advice, and naming the direct model. These are flagged as "flaky" for both, since even the better-performing variant only succeeded once in three tries. This suggests the capability is only partially present for with_skill and effectively absent for without_skill in this sample, but the small sample (3 runs) limits confidence in the exact rates.

Runtime and cost: very close between variants — without_skill ran ~4s faster (1m4s vs 1m8s) and cost slightly less (~$0.54 vs ~$0.57). Context window utilization was low for both (4.8% vs 5.9%), with no compaction needed. These differences are minor and not practically meaningful on their own.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs evaluated, all 3 skipped), so no direct quality comparison data is available.

Output consistency: without_skill showed "mostly_consistent" behavior across repeated runs (score 2.0, high confidence), with 1 dimension consistent, 1 mostly consistent, and 1 inconsistent — indicating some run-to-run variability even within without_skill. No consistency data was available for with_skill (marked null), so no comparison can be made on this dimension.

Overall state: On the assertions and expected-output measures where both variants could be compared, with_skill passed more often than without_skill, particularly on the core behavior of identifying direct model invocation and citing account-specific evidence — though both variants struggled with this behavior overall (at most 1/3 runs), so this should be read as a shared weakness with with_skill showing a partial edge rather than a solid capability gap. Two assertions showed no difference at all (both always passed), underscoring that not every check differentiates the variants. Runtime, cost, and context usage were comparable between variants. Quality comparisons and with_skill's output consistency could not be assessed due to skipped/missing data, leaving meaningful gaps in the overall picture.
